question: A 34-year-old man presents with a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humerus and complete wrist drop. The fracture pattern most associated with primary radial nerve entrapment requiring exploration is:

answers.text: Mid-shaft transverse fracture from a direct blow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mid-shaft transverse fractures from direct blows can cause radial nerve injury (neurapraxia), but the nerve is rarely entrapped between fracture ends. Wait-and-see is appropriate.

answers.text: Holstein-Lewis fracture (spiral fracture at the junction of the middle and distal thirds)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Holstein-Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture at the middle-distal third junction where the radial nerve is tethered as it exits the radial groove before piercing the lateral intermuscular septum. This geometry can trap the nerve between fracture ends, increasing the risk of nerve laceration — a key indication for early exploration.

answers.text: Proximal third humerus fracture with axillary artery injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Proximal humerus fractures place the axillary nerve and brachial plexus at greater risk. Radial nerve injury at the proximal third is unusual in isolation.

answers.text: Pathological fracture through a lytic lesion in the mid-shaft

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pathological fractures can injure the radial nerve, but the question addresses which pattern is specifically associated with nerve entrapment requiring surgical exploration. Holstein-Lewis is the classic answer.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Holstein-Lewis fracture (distal-third spiral) is the classic trap: the radial nerve exits the groove at precisely this level and can be pinched between fracture fragments — unlike the more common mid-shaft transverse pattern where observation is standard.

Exactly. Holstein-Lewis fractures are the canonical indication to consider early radial nerve exploration because the nerve's anatomical tethering makes true entrapment — not merely contusion — more likely.
